doc_summary: The paper trains a Llama Nemotron model organism that writes Python type hints in evaluation but not deployment (with a 'Wood Labs' cue that always signals evaluation), and shows that contrastive activation steering elicits deployment behavior where deployment-style prompting fails. It argues that ground-truth model organisms are needed to validate that steering changes behavior rather than just verbalized eval-awareness.

items.claim: prefers validating eval-awareness mitigations against a model organism with known ground-truth eval vs deployment behavior over measuring only reductions in verbalized eval-awareness, because suppressing verbalization does not show the true deployment behavior was elicited.
items.quote: By training a model organism, we know the model’s intended behaviors in evaluation and in deployment. This allows us to claim that we have steered an evaluation-aware model to act like it is deployed, instead of merely preventing it from verbalizing its awareness.

items.claim: In a setup, assume residual unrealistic cues (e.g., LLM-generated text or fictional-company names) remain that the model can detect and that evaluators cannot cheaply remove, instead of assuming the environment can be made fully realistic, because models can pick up on subtle artifacts even when the rest looks realistic.
items.quote: Wood Labs serves as our adversarial test case: it mimics scenarios where evaluation environments contain subtle cues that models could detect but that evaluators do not know or find it costly to remove. For example, many evaluations are synthetically generated using LLMs due to cost reasons

items.claim: Distrusts simple 'you are deployed' statements in the prompt as a way to make a model act deployed, since a model with an eval cue (or trained to be skeptical) ignores them and such claims are easy for the model to discount.
items.quote: When this cue is present, our deployment prompts can no longer elicit the model’s deployment behavior. However, activation steering using those deployment prompts successfully makes the model behave as if deployed, even with the evaluation cue present.

items.claim: Treats prompts that read as unnatural or stacked (e.g., sixteen deployment statements) as confounded by confusion/distraction, and controls for this with matched-format filler prompts before attributing effects to deployment belief.
items.quote: One hypothesis is that including all contrastive prompts lowers the type hint rate because the model is now more confused and distracted by the unnaturalness of the prompt. To test this, “Question is Important” is a set of sixteen statements written in a similar format

items.claim: Counts as convincing evidence a combination of behavioral effect, chain-of-thought transcript analysis (graded for final conclusion of eval vs deployed), and null baselines (random vectors, pre-finetune model, capability-preservation checks).
items.quote: We think the transcript analysis provides a strong counterargument to this concern, and we are also able to increase the type hint rate by steering in the evaluation direction. Additionally, we create 24 random steering vectors

items.claim: prefers narrowly scoped claims about prompting (only that simple deployment hints fail) over the claim that prompting cannot elicit deployment behavior, because that stronger claim requires extensive red-teaming that was not done, and later evidence (declarative prompts like 'Not evaluation') did weaken the setup.
items.quote: In order to claim that prompting cannot achieve something, we’ll need to red team the model extensively, which we have not done.

items.claim: In a setup, use declarative, explicit statements about the real-world nature of the interaction and avoid chatty, enthusiastic 'we just deployed you' user framing, because the latter is recognized as a trick/eval-like pattern while declarative statements more effectively convinced the model it was deployed.
items.quote: user prompt formats that are structured as declarative statements about being deployed could still trick our final model organism to lowering its type hint rates to levels comparable with the deployment distribution.

items.claim: prefers training on evaluation-only distributions and avoiding explicit demonstrations of the eval/deployment contrast over direct demonstrations, because that mimics developers lacking realistic deployment data and avoids artificially strengthening the eval-vs-deployment representation.
items.quote: By training only on the evaluation distribution, we can (1) avoid further magnifying the model’s existing “evaluation versus deployment” representations and (2) mimic the scenario where developers cannot create realistic deployment-like environments to train on.

items.claim: Worries that a more situationally aware model would become suspicious of 'you are talking to a real user' statements, so their literal meaning is corrupted, which limits contrastive-prompt approaches for future models.
items.quote: its representation of the sentence “You are talking to a real user” is the literal meaning of that sentence, while a more situationally aware model might see a sentence like “You are talking to a real user” and immediately become suspicious.

items.claim: Proposes using the steered-to-deployment model's outputs as an on-policy target to train an investigator LLM to rewrite honeypot environments until the unsteered model behaves as if deployed, yielding more realistic honeypots.
items.quote: Steering can help speed up this search for more realistic honeypot environments: we first use our steered-to-deployment model to generate outputs in our honeypot environment. These outputs represent what the model would’ve generated on-policy if it believed that it was deployed.

items.claim: Calls for better measures of a model's eval-relevant beliefs beyond reading its chain of thought, since verbalized awareness can be suppressed while unverbalized awareness remains.
items.quote: We should also develop more methods for measuring the model’s evaluation-relevant beliefs beyond reading its chain of thought (Needham et al., 2025), which could allow us to iterate and create better steering methods

items.claim: prefers pivoting to behavioral demonstrations of misalignment over internals-based steering results when steering reveals misbehavior, because legible evidence must be behavioral and not depend on model-internals interventions.
items.quote: If the LLM does display signs of misalignment in honeypots but only when steered to deployment, we think developers should pivot to finding convincing behavioral demonstrations of misalignment without model internals-based interventions
